paragraphs: In February 2025, for one month, I studied at the University of Glasgow in Scotland. I did my clerkship at the Glasgow Royal Infirmary in Glasgow.

I rotated for one month through orthopedics at the Glasgow Royal Infirmary, a hospital in the city of Glasgow. Because the supervising doctor's specialty was foot and ankle surgery, I mainly did my clerkship in the area of the ankle and foot. The flow of a day was a conference at 8 a.m. every morning where we all confirmed the operating schedule and policies, then going straight to the operating room, doing about three operations a day, such as total hip replacement and operations fixing the ankle with bolts and so on, and dispersing around 17:00. The supervising doctor was a person from Jordan, for whom English is a second language, but his English was very fluent and easy to understand, so I thought I should do my best too. He let me into the operative field every day and explained each step, which was very educational. When one studies abroad in an English-speaking country, almost all communication is in English, and I thought that is a very big advantage. By placing myself in an environment where I had no choice but to speak English, I think I was able to improve my English. Also, the UK has a healthcare system different from Japan's. Most British people use the National Health Service, the NHS, to receive care. To be seen under the NHS, one first receives a diagnosis from a family doctor called a GP (General Practitioner), and is referred to a specialist hospital as needed. This NHS has no consultation fee, but correspondingly waiting times are long, and there is the problem that patients cannot quickly access the care they need. Many of the patients I saw in the outpatient clinic were in a state where symptoms had worsened to a degree one would not see in Japan. Because the funding source is taxes, the supervising doctor's attitude of trying to use the cheapest possible bolts in surgery was also impressive. Between operations I waited in the waiting room, and during that time I was able to hear various stories about differences in healthcare systems between countries and about doctors' treatment and salaries, which was a very good opportunity. In Jordan, doctors' salaries are apparently far higher than other occupations, but lower compared with the UK, so that doctor moved to the UK, but he said that the rules for a foreigner to work as a doctor in the UK are strict and it is hard. Being able to hear many stories from the viewpoint of an overseas doctor was also a very good experience.

I am sensitive to cold, and since I had heard that February in Glasgow is very cold, I wore Uniqlo Super Warm Heattech and an ultra light down, and on top of that a down jacket, and I never thought it was cold, which was a relief. For housing, I rented an Airbnb about a 15-minute walk from the hospital and commuted from there. When keeping costs down, the style of living with the host or others is common, and I also stayed in such lodging. We watched soccer together while eating pizza, and sometimes they cooked dishes from various countries and we had dinner together, which was actually a good experience. Also, because others lived there too, most daily necessities were provided, so there was no need to go shopping on the first day, which I found convenient. I think the real pleasure of studying abroad is talking with local people and becoming friends, so I thought this style suited me. Eating out is expensive, so I mostly bought ingredients at a supermarket called Lidl and cooked for myself. The hospital I went to had no canteen, so local people and hospital staff too mostly cooked for themselves and brought packed lunches. On the first day I arrived in Glasgow, a medical student from the University of Glasgow who had similarly come to Nagoya University invited me to dinner and treated me to Italian food. After that I had several more chances to meet, and I was able to spend very meaningful time learning the thinking of a medical student from a foreign country. Also, Dr. Alec Logan, a GP, took me to various events. The day I arrived in Glasgow I received contact from him, and the next day we went together to a Celtic match, where I saw the Japan national team players Daizen Maeda and Hatate up close and was able to feel the local atmosphere. We went to a Celtic away game, and since the stadium was small the pitch was close and it felt immersive and was very interesting. The local supporters were heckling and so on, and I could feel real home-of-football soccer. In addition, I was invited several times to films and opera and so on, and was able to experience a culture different from Japan. He also let me observe the actual outpatient clinic at Dr. Alec's clinic and explained various things about the GP system, which was a good opportunity to think about healthcare systems. I am truly grateful that he arranged opportunities that I could not have had on my own.

I applied to this clinical study abroad program out of light interest at first, but as I went on I had to prepare a CV and a statement of purpose and find and reserve my own housing and prepare supplies, so it was harder than I expected, and money and time are also needed in large amounts, so the burden is large, but I thought studying abroad is worthwhile. I think there are definitely experiences that can be gained only by studying abroad, and I think there were parts of me that grew by meeting various people. Finally, I would like to sincerely thank the doctors of the International Collaboration Office who gave me such a valuable opportunity and everyone who supported me.
For five weeks from March to April 2025, I studied at the Seoul National University College of Medicine.

I did my clerkship at Seoul National University Hospital. For the first three weeks I rotated through transplant and vascular surgery, and for the last two weeks plastic surgery. In the clerkship in transplant and vascular surgery, on Mondays and Tuesdays arteriovenous fistula operations for dialysis were performed, and on the other days I was allowed to observe operations such as kidney transplantation and varicose veins. Depending on the doctor, some let me into the operative field. I had observed liver transplant surgery at Nagoya University Hospital but had never seen kidney transplantation, so it was a very good opportunity. Conversation among staff was mainly in Korean, but not only doctors but also nurses and others could speak English, so I had no trouble communicating. At Seoul National University Hospital, two operating room nurses were assigned to each operation and did suturing and so on. In Japan, the image that doctors do such procedures is strong and I had hardly seen such a scene, but the doctors said that behind this is the strike against the increase in medical school enrolment taking place in Korea. As a result, the number of working doctors was insufficient, and instead they increased the number of operating room nurses. In fact, I was surprised to hear that when I visited there were no residents and professors and others were taking night duty. Also, compared with Japan the operating times were short, and I felt that perhaps Japan does things more carefully. Other exchange students from Japan said the same thing, so I thought that on the whole operations in Japan take more time.

The head of plastic surgery was a Professor Chang, who graduated from the Keio University School of Medicine and could converse in Japanese, which I was very grateful for. I was allowed to observe operations such as breast reconstruction and, in children, polydactyly and cleft palate. Since he was a doctor who graduated from a Japanese medical school, it was a familiar style of asking students questions like in a polyclinic. When I asked questions he taught me various things, which was very educational. As an exchange student I am in a position where kind doctors will teach me even if I am passive, but I thought the most important thing is to ask questions actively about anything to show that I am motivated and to have an attitude of trying to communicate. In the last week, Seoul National University medical students returned to the clerkship and I had a chance to talk with them a little. When I listened to them, they apparently had been advancing to the next year even while not attending clerkships, and their upcoming clerkship and study plans seemed hard.

I could not use the Seoul National University dormitory, so I secured lodging through Airbnb five minutes' walk from the medical school campus. The nearest station is Hyehwa Station, and access to Dongdaemun and Myeongdong is also good. Around Hyehwa Station there are about three universities, so it is a town with very many students, and perhaps because of that there are also many stylish restaurants. Korean lodgings basically have no bathtub, only a shower, and the place I booked was also one room within an apartment unit, with a separate toilet and shower but a shared kitchen and washing machine. There are often tourists in the neighbouring rooms too, and you can hear voices, so some people may feel cramped. There are also cases where it is not written that the kitchen and so on are shared, which is hard to tell, and I misunderstood this and was confused. For meals, I went to a supermarket called Homeplus and bought meat and vegetables and cooked them. Since there was no rice cooker, I substituted packaged rice or pasta for carbohydrates. Except when eating with friends I mostly managed with cooking for myself, but there are many delicious Korean restaurants around Hyehwa Station and near Dongdaemun, so if you have the leeway, I think it is good to try eating out. Overall they are not that expensive and the taste suits Japanese people. However, dishes such as dak-hanmari and samgyeopsal are for two servings and up, so you may not be able to order them alone.

On weekends and on days when the clerkship ended early, I ate ganjang gejang and went to a jjimjilbang, a traditional Korean sauna, with friends who had similarly come from Nagoya University for a clinical clerkship at Korea University. In addition, a pharmacist working at Seoul National University and the doctors of plastic surgery, whom I met locally, took me out for meals and taught me various things about Korean culture and circumstances, which became an irreplaceable experience.
